strengths: The ESD/span profile framework is a clean, signal-aware reformulation of statistical complexity for spectral algorithms that avoids source conditions and eigenvalue-decay assumptions, and the paper convincingly argues why existing signal-agnostic measures (effective dimension d_eff(ν), Bartlett et al.'s k*) cannot capture alignment effects (Section 3.1, Section 10.1 sparse-signal example).

The minimax results are coherent and matched: Theorem 3.2 (PC estimator risk bracketed by (d†-1)σ² and 2d†σ²) plus Theorem 3.3/4.3 (lower bound via Assouad's method) establish that ESD is the canonical complexity index up to constants for the considered model classes, and Theorem 4.1's quota-sequence regularity conditions are mild and easily verified (Example 4.2).

The extensions are substantive rather than perfunctory: the whitening reduction for correlated noise (Section 8.1), the SVD-based equivalence for fixed-design linear regression (Section 8.2-8.3), and the careful treatment of the random-design RKHS setting (Section 9), where the inflation of the effective noise variance by ||f*||²∞/n and the (K,n)-regularity condition (Assumption 9.4) are handled honestly and Example 9.7 correctly recovers the classical n^{-sβ/(1+sβ)} rate.

Section 5 provides a genuinely insightful negative result: the formalization of the ridge saturation effect via the ridge saturating dimension d^Δ (Theorem 5.6, Example 5.7) rigorously explains why any ridge-calibrated complexity index cannot characterize intrinsic difficulty when s > 2, which supports the paper's choice of a PC-crossing-based measure.

The numerical experiments (span profile evolution under OP-GF, ESD vs. oracle PCR/KPCPE risk, pathwise ESD for a deep linear network) are well aligned with the theory and empirically confirm the proportionality between ESD and oracle risk (Figures 1-5).

The limitations are candidly stated: the OP-GF analysis covers only eigenvalue learning (fixed eigenbasis), the RKHS extension assumes known computable eigenfunctions, and Theorem 6.2's setting is restricted.
weaknesses: The core ESD definition is essentially the truncation point where the squared signal tail equals the noise variance, which is a natural but fairly simple quantity; the minimax rate Kσ² over these classes is arguably anticipated from classical sequence model theory (Johnstone [24]), so the conceptual novelty is more a reparameterization/unification than a fundamentally new technique, and the paper's strongest claims of generality are not fully realized in the analysis.

Theorem 6.2, the paper's main adaptive-learning result, carries a very restrictive and intricate set of side conditions (four conditions, including a complicated subset-cardinality balancing condition 4 involving A1, B1, B2), and the conclusion d†(t2) ≤ d†(t1) is a qualitative monotonicity statement over a narrow time window [t1, t2) with a delicate initialization b0; the practical reach of this result is unclear and the conditions are hard to interpret or verify.

Only the PC estimator is analyzed in the extended settings; ridge and gradient-flow filters are defined (Equations 5-6) but never given upper bounds, so the framework's minimax rate statements rest entirely on the PC/KPCPE benchmark, and the treatment of ridge is exclusively negative (Section 5). This narrows the claimed scope of 'spectral algorithms.'

In the RKHS extension the effective noise level σ² = (σ²0 + ||f*||²∞)/n depends on the target f* itself, so the class F^(n)_{K,k} (Equation 29) is defined through a quantity involving the unknown signal; the resulting minimax characterization is therefore somewhat circular and weaker than a genuine distribution-free adaptivity statement.

The RKHS reduction requires a bounded target (Assumption 9.1) and only a heuristic control of the design-induced variance; the claimed sharpness of the sequence-model rate in Section 9 (Theorem 9.5/9.6) needs the (K,n)-regularity condition whose compatibility with the class definition is not deeply explored beyond Example 9.7.

The experiments are entirely synthetic and small-scale (n = 300-1000, d up to 5000-9000); no real-data application is given to demonstrate that the ESD diagnostic is informative for practical adaptive kernel or neural network training beyond deep linear networks.

Presentation is marred by systematic labeling errors: assumptions and conditions are repeatedly referred to as theorems ('Suppose Theorem 6.1 holds' for Assumption 6.1, 'Under Theorem 5.2' for Assumption 5.2, 'Theorem 4.1 ensures' for Condition 4.1, 'Theorem 8.1' for Definition 8.1, 'Theorem 9.2'/'Theorem 9.4' mislabels), 'Theorem 3.4' versus 'Example 3.4' inconsistency, and a statement in Section 10.1 that the covariance-splitting index k* is 'covariance-splitting' misnamed; these errors, while not affecting correctness, suggest insufficient proofreading of a long manuscript.

The lower bound in Theorem 3.3 and proofs of Theorems 4.3/9.5/9.6 rely on nearly identical Assouad constructions, with 'the rest of the proof is identical and is omitted' phrasing; the proof appendix is functional but largely assembly of standard arguments, limiting the technical depth contribution.

strengths: The paper develops a coherent framework: the ESD and span profile give a clean, signal-aware way to quantify bias-variance trade-offs for spectral algorithms, and Theorem 3.2/3.3 establish that the Kσ² rate is minimax optimal over ESD-defined classes, including settings where classical eigen-decay or source conditions do not apply.

The examples (Example 3.4, Example 4.4) show that the framework recovers classical rates as special cases and can identify settings (e.g., logarithmic corrections) where source-condition-based rates are non-sharp, which is a useful contribution beyond existing theory.

The analysis of why ridge-based complexity indices fail due to the saturation effect (Section 5) is a nice conceptual contribution, and the lower bound for ridge risk (Theorem 5.6) is a concrete formalization.

Numerous cross-model extensions (fixed-design linear regression via SVD/whitening, RKHS regression via the Gram-matrix decomposition in Section 9) are carried out with explicit assumptions, and the proofs provided in the appendix appear largely correct at the level checked, with standard but carefully executed arguments (Assouad's method, hitting-time analysis of the OP-GF ODE).
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the core results: the central minimax claim (Theorem 3.3) is essentially the classical Gaussian sequence model result — classes defined by squared tail energy at cutoff K, with truncation/PC estimation achieving Kσ² — and the lower bound proof is a textbook Assouad construction over hypercube vertices on the K leading coordinates. The framing of ESD as 'the canonical complexity measure' is partly self-referential: a class defined by a quantity will trivially have its minimax rate characterized by that quantity.

The ESD depends on the unknown signal θ*, so it cannot be computed from data and serves only as a post-hoc diagnostic; the paper acknowledges this but the practical significance of the 'alignment-sensitive' theory is thereby diminished.

The extensions rely on assumptions that weaken the headline claim of 'no source or eigen-decay conditions.' The RKHS treatment requires a bounded target (Assumption 9.1), inflates the effective noise by ‖f*‖²∞/n (which can dominate σ₀²), and imposes a new, nontrivial regularity condition (Assumption 9.4) to get minimax lower bounds — so the theory is not as assumption-free as advertised.

Theorem 6.2, the main result connecting feature learning to ESD reduction, comes with four highly intricate conditions involving many unspecified constants, signal-gap conditions, and set-cardinality constraints (condition 4) on quantities that depend on the unknown θ* and the trajectory itself. It is unclear whether these conditions are verifiable or even plausible in realistic settings, which substantially limits the significance of the central claim that gradient flow provably reduces the ESD.

The experimental evidence is thin: only small-scale synthetic simulations (sequence models with d=5000, n=10000; a single deep linear network run), 10–20 Monte Carlo replications, no real data, and no comparison against alternative alignment measures. The experiments largely illustrate the theory (oracle risk tracks d†) rather than test it in regimes where classical theory fails.

Substantial presentation and polish problems that undermine confidence: pervasive cross-referencing errors ('Suppose Theorem 6.1 holds' should be Assumption 6.1; 'Under Theorem 5.2' should be Assumption 5.2; 'defined in Theorem 8.1' and 'Theorem 9.2' refer to a definition; 'Property (3) in Theorem 3.6' vs Proposition 3.6; 'Proof of Theorem A.1' for Lemma A.1; duplicated references [5]/[6]; the phrase 'we kindly remind the reader'). These errors occur in statements of results and assumptions, not just cosmetic text.

Reproducibility is inadequate: no code or supplementary materials appear to be released, and experimental details (e.g., how λ̃(t) is estimated, exact gradient flow discretization, hyperparameter choices for the linear network) are incomplete.

The manuscript is diffuse: a large portion (Sections 8–10, Appendix D) is extension and illustration material, while the technically novel and difficult part (Section 6, Theorem 6.2) is the least convincing due to its restrictive conditions; eigenfunction evolution for learned kernels is deferred entirely to an empirical sketch and future work.

strengths: The ESD/span-profile framework is a clean and well-motivated complexity measure: being signal-, spectrum-, and noise-aware, it genuinely distinguishes signal-kernel alignment, unlike classical signal-agnostic measures (deff(ν), effective rank k*); Section 3.2 and Section 10.1 give concrete examples where ESD separates spectra that those measures cannot.

The minimax characterization (Theorems 3.3 and 4.3) is correct and matched up to constants, proved via a straightforward but carefully executed Assouad/Fano argument with explicit regularity conditions (Condition 4.1) on the quota sequence.

The paper honestly positions ESD as a population-level diagnostic rather than a training input, and the discussion of estimator-guided indices (Section 5, ridge saturation, Theorem 5.6) is a genuinely useful contribution that rigorously explains why ridge-calibrated complexity fails to be intrinsic.

Extensions are done with reasonable care: the whitening reduction for correlated noise (Section 8.1), the explicit Gram-matrix decomposition in the RKHS case with variance inflation (Section 9), and the PSD-kernel modification in Remark 9.8 show the authors anticipated obvious objections.

Numerical experiments (Figures 1-5) are aligned with the theory and empirically confirm the risk bounds in the linear and RKHS settings; the recovery of the classical n^{-sβ/(1+sβ)} rate (Example 9.7) and the sharper logarithmic rate (Example 4.4) show the framework both recovers and refines classical results.
weaknesses: The core contribution is technically light. The ESD is essentially the bias-variance crossing point of spectral truncation, and the minimax result over the induced classes re-derives classical diagonal-sequence/ellipsoid results (Johnstone [24]) under a different parameterization. The primary novelty is conceptual reformulation rather than new mathematical machinery, which limits the significance for a main-track theory paper.

The central adaptive-learning claim rests on a weak result. Theorem 6.2 (OP-GF reduces ESD) holds only between two time points, under a set of unusually heavy and hard-to-verify conditions (in particular condition 4, involving subset cardinality inequalities over A1, B1, B2 that are opaque and likely nongeneric). The result establishes non-increase of d† at one time rather than a robust, quantitative ESD reduction guarantee, so the headline connection between feature learning and provable generalization gains is under-supported relative to the abstract's claims.

Analysis of kernels with evolving eigenfunctions is deferred to a small empirical demonstration (Section 10.2, deep linear networks), so the paper does not deliver a rigorous theory for the setting (learned kernels) that motivates it; the abstract's claim of studying 'spectral algorithms... where kernels are learned from data' is stronger than what is proven.

The RKHS extension inflates the effective noise to σ² = (σ0² + ||f*||∞²)/n and the minimax lower bound requires a (K,n)-regularity condition (Assumption 9.4) on the spectrum; together these conditions partially undermine the claim that the framework applies 'without spectral assumptions' — the finiteness/regularity requirement is simply moved elsewhere, and the ||f*||∞-dependent variance makes the bound loose unless ||f*||∞ ≲ σ0.

Significant presentation and editorial defects: pervasive cross-referencing errors (Assumption 6.1 called 'Theorem 6.1', Assumption 5.2 called 'Theorem 5.2', Condition 4.1 called 'Theorem 4.1', Definition 8.1 referenced as 'Theorem 8.1', Lemma C.4 referenced as 'Theorem C.4', etc.), a duplicated reference ([5]=[6]), 'Theorem 9.4 is a mild condition' referring to an assumption, and low-resolution figures (Figures 2 and 5 have unreadable axis labels). These errors make the manuscript hard to trust and verify without substantial reader effort.

ESD depends on unknown population quantities (θ*, σ², and in RKHS the full spectrum and eigenfunctions); the paper concedes it is 'for theoretical analysis rather than a training input'. Consequently there is no algorithmic payoff, and the practical relevance for real adaptive kernel methods (where eigenfunctions/eigenvalues are not explicitly available) remains speculative.

Some derivations are informal where rigor would matter: the reduction in Equation (3) motivating the sequence model relies on a law-of-large-numbers heuristic (the rigorous treatment is deferred and requires bounded f*), and several proofs in the OP-GF appendix (e.g., Part 3 of the proof of Theorem 6.2) are sketchy, with phrases like 'for c is small and C is large enough' substituting for explicit constant tracking.

strengths: The Effective Span Dimension is a clean, well-motivated, noise-indexed complexity measure that captures signal–spectrum alignment; it is well-defined for arbitrary kernels and signals without eigen-decay or source conditions, which is genuinely useful for analyzing learned kernels.

The minimax theory is rigorous and complete: matching upper and lower bounds (Theorems 3.3, 4.3, B.3, C.7, C.8) are proved via Assouad's method with careful quota-sequence regularity conditions, and the framework recovers classical rates (Proposition E.6, Example C.9) while producing new instances the classical framework cannot capture (e.g., the logarithmic rate in Example 4.4).

The related-work treatment is unusually thorough and honest (Appendix A): the paper clearly distinguishes ESD from balanced spectral cutoffs/early stopping, signal-agnostic effective dimensions, and alignment measures, and even proves (Appendix I) why a ridge-guided alternative fails due to saturation, pre-empting an obvious reviewer question.

The adaptive result (Theorem 5.2) makes a genuine step beyond Li & Lin (2024) by connecting OP-GF dynamics to provable ESD reduction, with substantial supporting analysis (Appendix G), a concrete verification example (Appendix H), and experiments (Figures 1–2) that consistently track the theory.

Extensions to fixed-design linear regression, correlated noise, and RKHS regression (Appendices B–C) are worked out with the necessary care (e.g., the effective noise variance accounting for the design-induced term, and the extension beyond the range of the integral operator).
weaknesses: The core minimax statements are close to classical sequence-model results: classes defined via the bias–variance crossing (Theorem 3.3) largely re-derive known results of Johnstone and Blanchard–Mücke in reparametrized form, so the novelty rests mainly on interpretation and the RKHS extension; the genuinely new rate phenomenon (Example 4.4) is somewhat niche.

The central adaptive claim (Theorem 5.2) is established only in a narrow setting: fixed eigenbasis, and the conclusion is merely a weak monotonicity d†(t2) ≤ d†(t1) at endpoint times, with no rate of ESD decrease, no post-adaptation risk bound, and Conditions (1)–(4) that are extremely intricate and hard to interpret. For evolving eigenfunctions — the setting of actual neural networks — only experimental evidence (Appendix D.2, Figure 5) is provided, and a general theorem is explicitly left open.

The OP-GF dynamics analyzed are directly borrowed from Li & Lin (2024); the contribution is the ESD lens rather than new dynamics, so the adaptive part is partly incremental relative to that line of work.

The bridge from RKHS regression to the sequence model (Equation 3) is heuristic; the rigorous treatment requires boundedness of f* and inflates the noise via ||f*||²∞/n (Appendix C), which weakens the punchline that ESD characterizes kernel regression 'without assumptions'.

Condition 4.1 restricts admissible quota sequences (increments ≤ 1, monotone k/Mk), so the asymptotic minimax result covers only a subclass of population classes; how restrictive this is for realistic alignment profiles is not fully discussed.
The ESD is a population quantity not computable in practice; the paper's suggestions for data-driven surrogates (Discussion) are speculative and untested, limiting practical significance.

Experiments are confined to synthetic sequence models and one deep linear network; no experiments on realistic kernels or data, so the claimed connection to neural network generalization remains largely motivational.

strengths: The ESD is a cleanly defined, noise-indexed, alignment-sensitive complexity measure, and the paper is admirably honest in Appendix A about its relationship to classical balanced spectral cutoffs, early stopping, effective dimension, and kernel-target alignment.

The minimax analysis is technically solid: Theorem 3.3/4.3 combine a simple bias-variance upper bound (via a fixed-cutoff PC estimator) with a standard Assouad hypercube lower bound, and the proofs in Appendices E–G are detailed and appear correct.

The paper correctly recovers classical rates under source/eigen-decay conditions (Examples 3.4–3.5, Example C.9) and gives a concrete case (Example 4.4) where the ESD-based rate is sharper than source-condition-based analysis.

Limitations are candidly discussed: the population-level nature of ESD, the open status of evolving-eigenfunction theory, and the absence of a post-selection oracle inequality for data-dependent kernels (Appendix A.1).
The appendix treatment (linear models, RKHS, correlated noise, ridge saturation in Appendix I) is thorough and shows genuine effort at completeness.
weaknesses: The central claim suggested by the title and abstract — minimax rates for 'spectral algorithms with learned kernels' — is not actually established for learned kernels. The theory freezes the spectrum at each time point, the ESD-reduction result (Theorem 5.2) covers only a fixed eigenbasis eigenvalue-learning model, gives only the weak endpoint comparison d†(t2) ≤ d†(t1) (non-increase, not strict reduction), and relies on a forbidding list of conditions (Conditions 1–4 with many sub-clauses and constant-inequality requirements). The evolving-eigenfunction case, which is what motivates neural networks, is left to a single deep-linear-network experiment.

There is a degree of circularity limiting the significance of the 'minimax' claims: the ESD-bounded class is defined by the very quantity whose minimax difficulty is measured, so the fact that the rate scales as σ²K largely reflects the standard bias-variance structure of PC/ridge truncation. The class F_{K,λ} is essentially a weak-ℓ-type/hyperbolic tail class, and Theorem 3.3's proof is a textbook Assouad argument; the genuinely new content is a repackaging of the known balanced-cutoff index into a 'complexity measure'.

The RKHS extension leans on the law-of-large-numbers bridge in Equation (3), which inflates the effective noise by ∥f*∥∞²/n and requires bounded targets plus an extra spectral regularity assumption (Assumption C.5); empirical spectra/eigenfunctions are explicitly not analyzed, further weakening the connection to actual (data-dependent) kernel learning.

Theorem 5.2's conditions (signal dichotomy at scale M vs. c'ε, no near-ties among strong coordinates, four sub-conditions on the learned spectrum at t1) are restrictive and hard to verify outside the specially constructed example in Appendix H; the theorem also depends on a specific initialization b0 and time horizon t2, so its practical import for adaptive methods is unclear.

Experiments are small-scale and purely synthetic (PC estimators in Gaussian sequence models with d=5000, one deep linear network run), and do not test real kernel learning, real data, or any estimator that actually uses ESD; Figure 5 is a single trajectory without repetitions.

Considering the modest conceptual novelty (a known bias-variance crossing rebranded as a signal-dependent dimension), the partially unsupported headline connection to learned/adaptive kernels, and the heavily conditioned adaptive result, the contribution falls short of the standard for the main track, though the careful appendices make it salvageable with substantial revision and a more honest narrowing of claims.

strengths: The core idea is clean and well-motivated: the ESD turns the classical bias–variance crossing into a population-level, signal-, spectrum-, and noise-dependent complexity measure, providing a minimax calibration (σ²K) that remains meaningful when classical source/eigen-decay assumptions are unavailable — a relevant question for adaptive/learned kernels.

The theory is technically solid: Theorem 3.3 and Theorem 4.3 give matching upper bounds (oracle PC estimator) and nontrivial minimax lower bounds via Assouad's method, with a genuinely nontrivial quota-sequence regularity condition (Condition 4.1) governing the n-dependent class; the log-corrections in Example 3.4(2) and the sharp source-ellipsoid embedding (Example 3.5) show the framework is calibrated against classical results rather than merely consistent with them.

The treatment of related work is unusually thorough and honest: Appendix A carefully disentangles ESD from balanced spectral cutoffs/early stopping, signal-agnostic effective dimensions, and target–kernel alignment measures, and Appendix I gives a concrete saturation-effect argument for why ridge-guided indices cannot serve as intrinsic complexity measures.

Limitations are candidly acknowledged: the rigorous adaptivity mechanism is established only for fixed-eigenbasis eigenvalue learning; the evolving-eigenfunction case is explicitly left open, with only a pathwise formulation and experiments provided.

The paper recovers classical rates (Examples 3.4–3.5, Theorems C.7–C.8, Example C.9), extends to linear and RKHS regression, and the experiments (Figures 1–5) directly support the ESD–risk connection and its evolution under over-parameterized gradient flow.
weaknesses: Limited novelty relative to prior work. The ESD is essentially the oracle truncation level of hard thresholding/PC regression, and the minimax characterization σ²K over tail-bounded classes is close to classical sequence-model results (Johnstone 2017; Birgé–Massart-style model selection) and to the oracle PC rates of Zhang et al. (2023). The paper acknowledges this ('the algebraic connection is not the novelty'), but the main theorems' incremental nature relative to these results weakens the significance of the contribution.

The central minimax results are somewhat self-referential: the classes F_{K,λ} are defined in terms of exactly the quantity (ESD) that the minimax risk is shown to scale with. Since H_{θ,λ}(k) is precisely the averaged squared tail energy, an ESD-bounded class is close to a standard ellipsoid/hyperrectangle constraint, so the linear σ²K rate is not surprising; the genuinely new content is the alignment-sensitive interpretation and the lower bound for n-dependent quotas, which is a modest addition.

The headline connection between adaptive learning and generalization is only partially established. Theorem 5.2 gives only a weak endpoint inequality d†(t2) ≤ d†(t1) under an extremely complicated set of conditions (page-long Condition (4) with many constants), it applies only to fixed eigenbasis eigenvalue learning in a sequence model, and the discussion honestly concedes that a theorem for evolving eigenfunctions remains open. Thus the link to neural networks / learned kernels is at this point largely conceptual plus synthetic experiments (deep linear networks), not a demonstrated phenomenon for realistic adaptive methods.

Condition (4) of Theorem 5.2 is essentially unverifiable in general and hurts readability; the main-text presentation of Theorem 5.2 is nearly impenetrable, and the illustrative verification (Appendix H) works only at the trivial initial time t1 = 0 where B2 = ∅ and A1 = ∅, which substantially weakens the claim that the conditions are practically checkable.

The reduction from RKHS regression to the sequence model (Equation 3) is heuristic in the main text and only justified under the bounded-target assumption (Assumption C.1), which inflates the noise by ∥f*∥∞²/n; the extension to general L² targets is handled only via an irreducible-bias convention. The RKHS lower bound additionally requires the (K,n)-regularity assumption and recovers the source-condition rate only for s ≥ 1 (Remark C.6), so the generality claim over classical theory is weaker than the framing suggests.

All experiments are synthetic sequence models, linear designs, and deep linear networks; no experiments on actual kernel adaptation (e.g., learned kernels of Li & Lin 2025) or real data are provided, so the empirical support for the paper's motivating narrative about neural networks is thin.

Reproducibility is limited: while the experimental settings are described, no code or repository link is mentioned, and the many unspecified constants in Theorem 5.2 would be difficult to instantiate.
